solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Pedal across river in pursuit of cold drink container (9)

indicators.note: something lying across a river spans it, so OF FEET stretches either side of PO
a pursuer comes behind, so the rest trails after C

blocks.note: C = cold, as on a tap
pedal means 'of the feet', read as OF FEET

annotation.surface: A cyclist pedals across a river after a cold drink.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pedal' looks like a verb for cycling; here it is the adjective, 'of the feet', which the setter splits into two words, OF FEET.
annotation.definitionFit: A compositional definition: coffee is the drink and the pot holds it.

entries.clue: One preparing The Trotters, perhaps, to go through at end of season? (5,4)

indicators.note: what comes at the end of something follows it, so COMB is placed after CURRY

blocks.note: to curry is to season with spice
to comb through = to go through thoroughly

annotation.surface: Someone getting The Trotters ready for the end of the season.
annotation.walkthrough: The Trotters sound like the family in the sitcom Only Fools and Horses; here they are trotting horses, and a currycomb is used to groom them.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example with a question mark: trotting horses are groomed with a currycomb, a stiff comb that prepares their coats.

entries.clue: Pilots conceal error in method of achieving height (7,4)

blocks.note: FO = flying officer, so pilots = FOS

annotation.surface: Pilots cover up a mistake made during a climb.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface sets up aircraft and altitude; the height is a high-jump bar, and the Fosbury flop is the backwards technique Dick Fosbury made famous in 1968.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the flop is the high-jump technique jumpers use to clear the greatest height.

entries.clue: Tidy last of autumn leaves, with none remaining? (5)

definitions.note: an adjectival phrase: food EATEN is food with none remaining

indicators.note: read as the verb 'departs', so the N goes out of NEATEN

blocks.note: the final letter of autumN, removed from the front of NEATEN

annotation.surface: Clearing up the last of the autumn leaves until none are left.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' looks like fallen foliage in the surface; it is the verb, telling the N to go.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic hint rather than a synonym: a dish that has been eaten has none remaining, hence the question mark.

entries.clue: Longed to hold court when making deal? (8)

indicators.note: a word that holds another has it inside, so PINED keeps WOO within

blocks.note: to court someone is to woo them

annotation.surface: Someone who longed to take the matter to court before agreeing a deal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Deal' reads as an agreement; it is also a timber word for softwood planks, often pine.
annotation.definitionFit: A timber-trade sense: deal is sawn softwood, pine or fir, so pinewood is deal by example.

entries.clue: Grumpy’s spurned by cold nymph (6)

indicators.note: to be spurned is to be rejected, so the C is thrown out

annotation.surface: A bad-tempered dwarf is turned away by a frosty nymph.
annotation.walkthrough: Grumpy's capital letter suggests the dwarf; it is just the adjective tetchy.
annotation.definitionFit: A classical example: Tethys, the Greek sea goddess and mother of the ocean nymphs, is often called a nymph herself.

entries.clue: Sportsman I hit when running who’s been put off his race? (13)

definitions.text: who’s been put off his race?

indicators.note: letters that are running are on the move, so they end up in a new order

annotation.surface: A runner, hit mid-race, has been put off his stride.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Race' reads as a running race; in the definition it is the human race, which a misanthropist has been put off.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic paraphrase: a misanthropist dislikes humankind, so he has been put off the human race.

entries.clue: Unruly mob issued Republican fliers (10)

indicators.note: an unruly crowd will not keep in line, so its letters break order

annotation.surface: A disorderly crowd hands out Republican leaflets.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fliers' looks like leaflets handed out by a political mob; it means birds.
annotation.definitionFit: A general term for a specific kind: mousebirds are small long-tailed African birds, and birds are fliers.

entries.clue: Writer from NZ, honestly, is rubbish (12)

indicators.note: something rubbish is badly made, so the letters need putting right

annotation.surface: A critic from New Zealand says, frankly, that a writer is no good.
annotation.walkthrough: The NZ and Z are what make this findable: few writers have a Z, and the Russian novelist has one.
annotation.definitionFit: A general term: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, author of The Gulag Archipelago, is a writer.

entries.clue: Remarkably, if periodically on foot, few delays (7)

indicators.note: what happens periodically happens at regular intervals, so take every second letter

blocks.note: the even letters: oN fOoT fEw DeLaYs

annotation.surface: Walking, surprisingly, causes few hold-ups.
annotation.walkthrough: Every second letter, starting from the N of 'on', spells the answer; the odd letters are filler.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: notedly means notably, in a way worth remarking.

entries.clue: Malpractice taking a heavy toll? (7,7)

blocks.note: the everyday sense: blatant overcharging, a rip-off
the literal sense: robbery on the highway, as a toll road that charges far too much

annotation.surface: Some wrongdoing that costs its victims dearly.
annotation.walkthrough: Highway robbery is the stock phrase for overcharging; the 'toll' makes it literal, as a charge for using a highway.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom made literal: highway robbery means gross overcharging, and an excessive road toll is exactly that.

entries.clue: Having no siblings? What’s more jolly! (4,3)

blocks.note: an only child has no brothers or sisters

annotation.surface: An only child finds life all the merrier for it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Jolly' looks like the adjective for cheerful; it is the British intensifier, as in 'jolly good', meaning very.
annotation.definitionFit: A British colloquial sense: jolly as an adverb means very, as does only too in 'only too glad'.

entries.clue: Preface, extremely short, chap’s withdrawn (11)

indicators.note: a word cut short loses its end, so VERY drops its Y

blocks.note: extremely = VERY, docked of its Y
Ted is any chap's name; the 's is 'has'

annotation.surface: A preface, brief to a fault, from a man who keeps to himself.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Short' sits beside 'extremely' so it looks like a description of the preface; it tells you to trim VERY.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an introverted person is withdrawn, turned inward.

entries.clue: Heavily defeat, causing upset in tie (4)

indicators.note: to upset something is to knock it over, so in a down clue it reads bottom to top

annotation.surface: A heavy loss that leaves the team upset after a tie.
annotation.walkthrough: Tonk is British slang for thrashing someone; KNOT turned over gives it.
annotation.definitionFit: British slang: to tonk a team is to trounce it.

entries.clue: Put back, in touching scene (5)

blocks.note: a set is the scene for a play or film

annotation.surface: Something put back in its place during a moving scene.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Touching' reads as moving or emotional; it is the old preposition meaning about, which RE also means.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to reset a bone or a clock is to put it back as it was.

entries.clue: Food fanatic hurt by obstruction (3,6)

blocks.note: a fitness nut is a fanatic
let = hindrance, as in 'without let or hindrance' and a tennis let

annotation.surface: A food fanatic is injured by something in the way.
annotation.walkthrough: LET as an obstruction survives in 'without let or hindrance' and the tennis call.
annotation.definitionFit: A general term: a nut cutlet, a vegetarian patty of chopped nuts, is a food.

entries.clue: Setter must have say, reflecting where ego comes from? (7)

indicators.note: a reflection is a mirror image, so EG reads back to front

blocks.note: ego is the Latin for I

annotation.surface: A crossword setter insists on having their say, betraying an ego.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Setter' in a crossword always tempts you to think of the compiler; here it is anything that makes a liquid set, like gelatin in a jelly.
annotation.definitionFit: A literal sense of a crossword word: gelatin makes jellies set, so it is a setter.

entries.clue: Acknowledgement that doctor’s up in his practice? (3,4,2,7,6)

definitions.text: Acknowledgement that doctor’s up in his practice?

blocks.note: read as praise for a GP who knows his stuff; meant as Holmes granting that Dr Watson is 'up in', well versed in, something
read as the doctor's surgery; meant as Holmes's own practice, his detective methods

annotation.surface: A patient notes that the doctor knows his job.
annotation.walkthrough: The doctor sounds like a GP in his practice; he is Dr Watson, and Sherlock Holmes says this line to him because Watson is 'up in', well versed in, Holmes's methods.
annotation.definitionFit: A quotation described: Holmes's line acknowledges that Dr Watson is versed in the detective's practice.

entries.clue: Amphetamine around a displaced person is something unwelcome (3,5)

indicators.note: one word placed around another surrounds it, so BENNY encloses A DP

blocks.note: a benny is slang for a Benzedrine (amphetamine) tablet

annotation.surface: Drugs around a refugee are an unwelcome thing.
annotation.walkthrough: A bad penny is the proverbial thing that always turns up, whether you want it or not.
annotation.definitionFit: A proverb: a bad penny always turns up, so the phrase names an unwelcome person or thing.

entries.clue: Living death, say, of old fool consuming variable amounts (8)

indicators.note: what is consumed is swallowed, so O MORON has XY inside

blocks.note: x and y, the algebra variables

annotation.surface: A fool, half alive, eats unpredictable helpings.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Living death' sounds like a horror film; it is the example, two contradictory words side by side.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: 'living death' pairs contradictory terms, the mark of an oxymoron.

entries.clue: The Dutch maybe with a life to envy! (5,4)

blocks.note: not the nation: Cockney 'my old Dutch' means one's wife, so a spouse
the well-off, whose lifestyle the rest of us watch enviously

annotation.surface: The Dutch people have a life others envy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The Dutch' is not the nation: 'my old Dutch' is Cockney for one's wife, one's other half.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: your other half is your spouse, like a Cockney's Dutch, and the other half are the well-off in 'how the other half lives'.

entries.clue: Turn to trivial attraction? Yes, if NY ultimately overrated somehow (8)

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so take the final letter
done somehow means done in some other way, so the letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: A cynic agrees New York is overrated if it becomes a tourist trap.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is about New York; the fodder is spelt out almost whole, so the hard part is believing DISNEYFY is a word.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: to Disneyfy is to make something into a sanitised, trivial theme-park attraction.

entries.clue: The end of cabbage-moth, its wings clipped back (5)

indicators.note: clipped wings are cut at the sides, so the outer letters go and the middle stays
going back means going the other way, so read right to left

annotation.surface: A cabbage moth meets its end with its wings clipped.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a real moth losing its wings; the wings are the letters on each side.
annotation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: omega is the last Greek letter, so 'Alpha and Omega' means the beginning and the end.

entries.clue: Pole, one travelling around in pursuit of good breeding stock (4,4)

indicators.note: letters that travel around wander from their places into a new order
a pursuer comes behind, so the anagram follows G

annotation.surface: A travelling Pole goes looking for good breeding stock.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pole' with a capital looks like a person from Poland; it is only fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A near-synonym: a gene pool is the stock of genes a breeding population carries.

entries.clue: Awkward, with tennis shot rebounding short (6)

indicators.note: a ball that rebounds comes back the way it went, so LOB turns to BOL

blocks.note: a lob is a high tennis shot
shy = short, as in 'two shy of a dozen'

annotation.surface: A tennis player sulks when a shot bounces back short.
annotation.walkthrough: Bolshy is British slang for stroppy, uncooperative; 'short' looks like it trims the shot, but it is the letters SHY.
annotation.definitionFit: British slang: someone bolshy is deliberately awkward and uncooperative.

entries.clue: Do you understand article extracted from ancient bit of Morse code? (6)

indicators.note: something extracted is pulled out, so the A leaves AGED

blocks.note: the dot in Morse is spoken as dit, the dash as dah

annotation.surface: Someone asks whether you follow an old scrap of Morse.
annotation.walkthrough: Geddit? is jokey spelling of 'get it?', said after a pun.
annotation.definitionFit: A colloquial spelling: geddit? is 'get it?', asking whether you understand the joke.

entries.clue: Celebrate with band, having relations over (5,2,2)

blocks.note: a hoop is a band, as round a barrel

annotation.surface: A party with a band where the relatives come over.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Band' plays to the party picture as musicians; it is a hoop. 'Relations' sounds like family; it is sex, IT.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal idiom: whooping is loud cheering, so whooping it up means partying noisily.

entries.clue: Waterproof cover to get bigger daily (3,5)

blocks.note: the moon waxes as it grows
a daily is a daily newspaper

annotation.surface: A cover for keeping things dry that seems to grow every day.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Daily' looks like an adverb; it is a noun, a daily paper.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: wax paper is coated to keep moisture out and is used to wrap food.

entries.clue: Field attack often using knight’s primitive weapon (9)

blocks.note: a sports field is a pitch
in chess a fork attacks two pieces at once, typically with a knight

annotation.surface: A battlefield charge led by a knight with a crude weapon.
annotation.walkthrough: The knight suggests medieval warfare; he is the chess piece, and the attack is a fork.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by use: the farm pitchfork is the improvised weapon of every angry mob.

entries.clue: To be received on board coach, he had to be wasted! (2,4,3,5)

indicators.note: a passenger on board is inside the vehicle, so HE'D goes inside TRAIN

blocks.note: a joke that goes down well is well received

annotation.surface: A coach passenger had to be drunk before boarding.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Coach' reads as a vehicle, which invites a bus; it is the verb, train. 'Wasted' as drunk is the surface; as squandered, the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: money or effort poured away like dirty water is lost for nothing.

entries.clue: Wages to take in combination with one’s printed currency (5,5)

indicators.note: to take in a lodger is to have them inside, so PAY has the rest within

blocks.note: perm = permutation, a combination of picks on a football pools coupon
the word itself, spelt out literally, with the 's dropped

annotation.surface: Wages paid with a combination of one's printed notes.
annotation.walkthrough: A perm, short for permutation, is the British football pools term for a set of combined forecasts.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: paper money is currency in the form of printed banknotes.

entries.clue: Confined to bed, I sat upright, lifting cast off (3,5)

indicators.note: what is confined is shut inside, so the answer lies within the words
lifting raises it, so in a down clue the letters read upward

annotation.surface: Someone stuck in bed sits up to lift off a plaster cast.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cast off' seems part of the picture, a plaster cast lifted away; it is the definition, meaning discarded.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to cast something off is to put it aside, discarding it.

entries.clue: Wryneck is a curse for one in the audience? (4)

indicators.note: an audience hears rather than reads, so the answer only has to sound like a word for a curse

annotation.surface: A twisted neck is the curse of anyone sitting in the audience.
annotation.walkthrough: Wryneck reads as a stiff neck; it is a woodpecker, Jynx torquilla.
annotation.definitionFit: A scientific name: Jynx is the genus of the wryneck, a woodpecker that twists its neck.

entries.clue: Religious court to risk row involving husband (4,3)

indicators.note: to involve is to take in, so H is taken into BET DIN

blocks.note: to bet is to risk money
a din is a row, a racket

annotation.surface: A court case about a gamble and a quarrel with a husband.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Row' could be a line or a quarrel; here it is a noise, a din.
annotation.definitionFit: A Hebrew term: beth din means 'house of judgement', a rabbinical court of Jewish law.

entries.clue: He worked with one fine Basque ruler’s famous visitor (5,2,5)

indicators.note: clay that is worked is kneaded into a new shape, and so are the letters

annotation.surface: A man worked alongside a fine Basque king's well-known guest.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Basque ruler' reads as one phrase; the ruler is King Solomon, and Basque is only fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A biblical allusion: the Queen of Sheba famously visited King Solomon.

entries.clue: Violent storm nearly closed navy yard? Not regularly (7)

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so take every other letter

blocks.note: a door that is 'to' is pushed nearly shut

annotation.surface: A storm nearly shuts a naval dockyard, though not on a regular basis.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not regularly' reads as 'irregularly'; in fact 'Not' is fodder and 'regularly' picks from 'yard? Not'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a tornado is a violent rotating windstorm.

entries.clue: Lodger when speaking knows Italian, apparently (6,3,2)

indicators.note: spoken aloud, the lodger word is heard rather than spelt

blocks.note: a roomer rents a room, a lodger
to have a language is to know it

annotation.surface: A lodger who speaks Italian, it seems.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Has' for 'knows' is the language sense: she has French.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: rumour has it means people say so, which is apparently so.

entries.clue: Round, empty space a copper’s left for cell (4)

indicators.note: read as the verb, departed, so A and CU leave VACUUM

blocks.note: A plus CU, the symbol for copper, both removed

annotation.surface: A policeman has gone, leaving an empty round cell.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Copper' and 'cell' suggest a police station; the copper is CU, the chemical symbol, and the cell is biological.
annotation.definitionFit: A biological sense: an ovum is an egg cell.

entries.clue: Assiduously if cheesily punned? (10)

definitions.note: the answer is a cheese; 'cheesily punned' says the adverb is a pun on one

indicators.note: a pun trades on a word's sound, so the adverb becomes a sound-alike

annotation.surface: Someone working diligently, if with a groan-worthy joke.
annotation.walkthrough: Caerphilly, a Welsh town, gives its name to a crumbly white cheese, and it is pronounced much like 'carefully'.
annotation.definitionFit: A pun in the cheese sense: Caerphilly is a cheese, which is what 'carefully' turns into when punned cheesily.

entries.clue: Second row to result from security at hospital? (4,7)

blocks.note: a lock for, or at, a ward
a ward is part of a hospital

annotation.surface: A second row of beds set out as part of hospital security.
annotation.walkthrough: The second row is a rugby union term: the two lock forwards pack down behind the front row of the scrum. Read literally, a lock for a ward is security at a hospital.
annotation.definitionFit: A rugby term: the lock forwards form the second row of the scrum.

entries.clue: After end of tea break catch folk not fully prepared (2,4-4)

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter
the anagram follows on after that letter
what breaks falls apart, so the letters re-form in a new order

annotation.surface: After tea, a break catches people unready.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tea break' reads as one thing; 'tea' gives a letter and 'break' is the anagram signal.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom from firearms: a gun at half-cock has its hammer only partly raised, so the phrase means not fully ready.

entries.clue: Later round mine fails to explode (9)

indicators.note: an explosion scatters the pieces, so the letters land in a new order

annotation.surface: Later on, a mine turns out to be a dud.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Round' looks like ammunition beside the mine; it is a stage of a competition.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the semifinal is a late round of a knockout competition.

entries.clue: Is French star briefly producing Godless book? (6)

indicators.note: something said briefly is cut short, so HERO loses its last letter

blocks.note: a star is a hero, docked of its O

annotation.surface: A French celebrity writes an atheist book.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Godless' sounds like atheism; it is a fact about the text, which never names God.
annotation.definitionFit: A biblical fact: the Book of Esther is the one book of the Hebrew Bible that never mentions God.

entries.clue: Host needing bedsit around Notting Hill for one (6)

indicators.note: one word around another surrounds it, so ROOM encloses MC

blocks.note: an MC, master of ceremonies, hosts a show
a bedsit is a single rented room

annotation.surface: A landlord in Notting Hill needs a bedsit.
annotation.walkthrough: Notting Hill is a London district, which the bedsit plays to; here it is the 1999 Hugh Grant film.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the film Notting Hill is a romantic comedy, a romcom.

entries.clue: Wrong opinion one’s to contradict, interrupting rather loudly (9)

indicators.note: an interruption breaks into something, so I'S BELIE breaks into MF

blocks.note: mf = mezzo forte, fairly loud, in music

annotation.surface: Someone loudly interrupts to contradict a wrong opinion.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rather loudly' looks like how the interruption is made; it is a musical dynamic, mezzo forte.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a misbelief is a mistaken belief.

entries.clue: Behind can be rested on twig? No chance! (6,2)

indicators.note: what rests on something sits on top of it, so in a down clue FOR goes above GET IT

blocks.note: to twig is to get it, to understand

annotation.surface: A bottom sitting on a twig? It's never going to work.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Behind' and 'twig' paint a backside on a branch; behind means supporting and twig means understand.
annotation.definitionFit: A colloquial refusal: forget it! means there is no chance of that.

entries.clue: Old priest cheated when clinching game (5)

indicators.note: a clinch is a tight hold, so DID holds RU inside

blocks.note: did = cheated, as in 'did him out of his money'

annotation.surface: A priest cheated to win a game.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Clinching' looks like winning the game; it is the container instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A historical sense: druids were the priests of the ancient Celts.

entries.clue: Reservoir I’m disgusted to find almost dry? (7)

blocks.note: a dam is a reservoir, the water held back
pish is an exclamation of disgust

annotation.surface: Someone is dismayed to find a reservoir nearly dried up.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is fair from the other side: what is almost dry is still a little damp.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition from the other end: slightly damp is also nearly dry, hence the question mark.

entries.clue: Old jail is empty, indeed (8)

annotation.surface: An old jail now stands empty.
annotation.walkthrough: Holloway was a London women's prison, closed in 2016, which is why it is 'old'.
annotation.definitionFit: A proper name: HM Prison Holloway in north London closed in 2016, so it is an old jail.

entries.clue: Reflecting determined, true character of Hamlet (7)

indicators.note: a reflection is a mirror image, so the letters read back to front

annotation.surface: A resolute, honest figure from Hamlet.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Character of Hamlet' could be the prince's personality; it is someone in the play.
annotation.definitionFit: A literary example: Laertes, Ophelia's brother, is a character in Hamlet.

entries.clue: Bill’s partner often eliminates cross females in culinary contests (4-4)

indicators.note: to cross something is to lie over it, so KOS spans FF

annotation.surface: Bill's partner knocks out angry women in cookery competitions.
annotation.walkthrough: Bill looks like a man's name; the partner is in the phrase 'bill and coo'. 'Cross' looks like angry, describing the females.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a cook-off is a cooking competition.

entries.clue: Tall touring basketball players refuse to go there (3,3)

indicators.note: a tour goes round a place, so BIG goes round NBA

annotation.surface: Tall basketball players on tour won't go somewhere.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' looks like the verb; it is the noun, rubbish, and a bin bag is where it goes.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: a bin bag is the place refuse goes.

entries.clue: Picture Greek going as a result of it? (3,7,2,4,6)

blocks.note: read as a painting; meant as a film, a 1990s British picture
read as a Greek departing; meant as ten letters that are themselves the scrambled name of a monarch
the answer describes an operation, and these words are what that operation produces

annotation.surface: A picture of a Greek, and what came of him.
annotation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: KING GEORGE rearranged gives 'Greek going', so the madness of King George produces the clue's words. It is also a 1994 film, the picture.
annotation.definitionFit: A film title: The Madness of King George is a 1994 picture about George III.

entries.clue: Mustard perhaps in that is revolting cause of illness (1,4)

indicators.note: COL is put in the other letters
a revolt overturns things, so IE is turned round to EI

blocks.note: Colonel Mustard of Cluedo, a colonel, COL

annotation.surface: Revolting mustard that makes you sick.
annotation.walkthrough: Mustard is Colonel Mustard from the board game Cluedo (Clue in the US), giving COL.
annotation.definitionFit: A medical fact: E. coli is a bacterium behind food poisoning.

entries.clue: Duck sounds like cat with its tail up (4)

indicators.note: a tail is the end of a word, and up in a down clue means the top, so the final S moves to the front

annotation.surface: A duck that makes cat noises with its tail in the air.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sounds like' is not a homophone here: a cat mews, and MEWS is its sounds.
annotation.definitionFit: A birdwatcher's example: the smew is a small diving duck.

entries.clue: Port from military canteen not available after one (7)

indicators.note: what comes after follows, so NA is written behind I

blocks.note: the mess is where the forces eat

annotation.surface: Port wine can't be had in the army canteen after one o'clock.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Port' reads as the drink beside a canteen; it is a harbour city.
annotation.definitionFit: A geographical example: Messina is a Sicilian port on the strait facing Italy's toe.

entries.clue: Work that’s both hard and I bet shattering (3,6)

indicators.note: something shattered is smashed into pieces, so the letters are reassembled

annotation.surface: A job that's tough and, you bet, exhausting.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Work' reads as labour, and 'shattering' as exhausting; the work is Tolkien's novel.
annotation.definitionFit: A literary sense: a work is a book, and The Hobbit is Tolkien's.

entries.clue: One from the Middle East, not long back (5)

indicators.note: going back means going the other way, so IN A MO reads right to left

blocks.note: 'not long' = in a mo, in a moment

annotation.surface: Someone from the Middle East returned recently.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not long back' reads as 'recently'; 'not long' is IN A MO, and 'back' reverses it.
annotation.definitionFit: A nationality: Oman is on the Arabian Peninsula, so an Omani comes from the Middle East.

entries.clue: Be alert! The first hunter possibly has returned? (5,4,4)

blocks.note: a hunter is a pocket watch with a lid, so the first hunter might be watch one

annotation.surface: A warning: the first hunter may be back.
annotation.walkthrough: A hunter is a pocket watch with a hinged cover, not someone with a gun.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to watch one's back is to stay on guard against danger.

entries.clue: Hear about girlfriend holding party after film triumph (3,4,2)

indicators.note: a hand holding something has it inside, so GF encloses the rest
what comes after follows, so DO is written behind ET WIN

annotation.surface: News reaches you of a girlfriend's party celebrating a film's success.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Party' looks political beside 'triumph'; it is a do, a celebration.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom from hunting: animals get wind of danger by scent, so to get wind of news is to hear of it.
